Reviewer #4:
In this study, Yulin Jin et al. have made great effort to conduct multi-omics strategy combined
with TWAS to decode the molecular mechanisms of FXTAS, and identified a novel prominent
driver gene of FXTAS pathogenesis, which is of significance for guiding its clinical practice.
However, there are also a number of issues which should be addressed.
1. The authors employed different criterion for the identification of DEGs at the onset of
phenotype (p<0.01), late progression stage (FDR<0.05) and for specific cell types (adjusted p-
value<0.05), is it reasonable? Are these identified DEGs comparable?
Thanks for raising this consideration. We acknowledge that our choice of thresholds differed
between analyses, reflecting specific experimental contexts and goals. At the early onset
stage, we used a nominal p-value threshold (p < 0.01) due to subtle transcriptional changes,
lower statistical power, and fewer DEGs at this stage. This criterion allowed us to detect
potential early gene expression changes that may be relevant to disease initiation. For
the late progression stage (bulk RNA-seq) and cell-type-specific analyses (snRNA-seq), we
applied a more stringent value (FDR < 0.05). At these stages, the number of DEGs was larger
and statistical power was greater, making it appropriate to use a conservative multiple-
testing correction to reduce false positives and focus on the most robustly altered genes.
Although the DEG sets were defined under slightly different thresholds, the comparisons we
highlight in the manuscript are made within each dataset rather than directly across
thresholds, and key findings (e.g., enrichment of neuronal pathways, overlap with TWAS
candidates) are consistent across approaches. Thus, while the DEG lists are not directly
interchangeable, the biological conclusions remain comparable and robust.

6. Why does the authors select TIGAR-V2 to conduct TWAS analysis, to my knowledge, several
tools such as PrediXcan and FUSION are more popular.
We thank the reviewer for raising this question. While PrediXcan (Gamazon et al., 2015) and
FUSION (Gusev et al., 2016) are widely used TWAS tools, we note that TIGAR and the
related TIGAR-V2 tool are also quite popular for TWAS (with the original TIGAR paper
having over 100 citations in Google Scholar). We chose TIGAR-V2 (Parrish et al., 2022) over
PrediXcan and FUSION as the former method has methodological flexibility and improved
performance over the latter two methods. PrediXcan and FUSION assume parametric priors
for modeling cis-eQTL effect sizes, which restrict their capability for handling complex
genetic architecture of transcriptomes. In contrast, TIGAR (Nagpal et al., 2019) employs a
nonparametric Bayesian method that provides a more flexible and general framework,
encompassing the parametric models used by PrediXcan and FUSION as special cases. Both
simulation studies and real data applications have demonstrated that TIGAR achieves higher
imputation accuracy of genetically regulated gene expression and greater statistical power to
detect associations with complex traits compared to PrediXcan and FUSION in TWAS
analyses. TIGAR-V2 extends the original TIGAR framework by incorporating parallel
computing to enhance computational efficiency. It can also accommodate both individual-
level and summary-level GWAS data, making it highly versatile for large-scale studies. Given
24
these advantages in modeling generalizability, imputation accuracy, and computational
efficiency, we chose TIGAR-V2 for our TWAS analyses.

We appreciate this thoughtful suggestion. In our model systems, the human FMR1 5′UTR-
CGG transgene is expressed at readily detectable levels in mouse brain tissues, as shown by
qRT-PCR and GFP-based snRNA-seq analyses (Fig. 4b; Supplementary Fig. 2e, f). Expression
was observed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, consistent with induction by the
strong CAG promoter. These data suggest that the transgene could produce sufficient CGG
repeat RNA to drive reproducible behavioral and neuropathological phenotypes. In parallel,
immunohistochemistry and western blot analyses confirmed accumulation of FMRpolyG
protein aggregates in the transgenic mouse brain (Fig. 4g,h), providing evidence that both
repeat RNA and its RAN-translated product are expressed at biologically relevant levels in
this model. We acknowledge, however, that the transgene RNA expression level represents
only a proxy for toxic RNA burden. The FMR1 5′UTR transgene produces both expanded
repeats RNA and FMRpolyG, and several molecular features, including secondary structures
(Broniarek et al., 2024), R-loop formation (Loomis et al., 2014), nuclear foci accumulation
(Hagerman et al., 2013), and RNA–protein interactions (Jin et al., 2007; Sofola et al., 2007;
Sellier et al., 2010), can affect the localization, stability, and function of repeat RNA. These
factors mean that measurable RNA abundance may not directly equate to pathogenic activity.

contributions of CGG repeats RNA versus FMRpolyG protein to the observed phenotypes.

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. In our study, we observed sex-specific differences
in disease onset and progression: male FXTAS mice exhibited earlier locomotor deficits,
whereas female mice showed delayed but progressive changes, including earlier onset of
weight gain. These findings parallel clinical observations in FXTAS patients, in which
penetrance, age of onset, and severity are generally higher in males than in females
(Hagerman & Hagerman, 2016). In humans, this sex difference is often attributed to the X-
linked nature of the FMR1 locus, with protective effects from the second X chromosome in
females. However, as the reviewer notes, our model employs an autosomal integrated
transgene under the control of a CAG promoter. Therefore, the observed sex-specific
phenotypes in mice cannot be explained solely by X-linked dosage compensation but may
instead reflect additional biological factors such as hormonal influences, metabolic
28
differences, or intrinsic sex-specific neuronal vulnerabilities. We have now incorporated this
point into the Discussion (Line 494-502).
